THE LANTERN HOUSE

CONTENTS

CHAPTER I. Arrival
CHAPTER II. The Letter
CHAPTER III. The Diamonds



CHAPTER I

ARRIVAL

On a grey afternoon in late October, Eleanor Vane came by the slow coach to Harrowgate, and from Harrowgate she walked the last mile to the lantern house on the cliff. The wind came off the sea in long cold breaths, and the gulls cried over the stone wall as if they were warning her away.

Mr. Thorne met her at the gate. He was a tall, stooping man with a lantern in one hand and a ring of iron keys in the other, and he said that the mistress of the house was resting and could not be disturbed. Eleanor Vane thanked him and followed him up the path between the dead roses.

"You will find the house very quiet," said Mr. Thorne. "We have not had a visitor since the spring. The old lady sleeps most of the day and walks most of the night."

Eleanor asked him how long he had kept the house. Mr. Thorne said that he had served the family for thirty years, and that he knew every board that creaked and every window that rattled. He showed her the kitchen, the long cold library, and the narrow stair to her room under the roof.

That evening Eleanor wrote in her journal by the light of a single candle. She wrote that Mr. Thorne was kind but watchful, that the library smelled of salt and old paper, and that somewhere below her a clock ticked very loudly. She wrote that she had been engaged to catalogue the library and that she meant to finish the work before the winter storms.

Before she slept she heard a door close softly on the floor below, and then the sound of slow footsteps going down toward the cellar. In the morning Mr. Thorne said that the house was full of noises and that she must not mind them.

Eleanor Vane spent the whole of the next day in the library. She found sea charts, books of sermons, a broken telescope, and a box of letters tied with black ribbon. She did not open the letters, because Mr. Thorne said that they belonged to the old lady and must not be touched.



CHAPTER II

THE LETTER

On the third morning a letter came from Harrowgate. It was from Dr. Crane, the physician who attended the old lady, and it said that he would call on Thursday to see his patient and to speak with the new librarian.

Dr. Crane arrived in a hired gig a little after noon. He was a small, quick man with spectacles and a cheerful voice, and he said at once that Eleanor looked pale and must take more air. Eleanor liked him immediately.

"Has Thorne shown you the cellar?" asked Dr. Crane, when they were alone in the library. Eleanor said that he had not, and that she had heard footsteps going down to it at night. Dr. Crane frowned and polished his spectacles and said nothing for a long while.

Then Dr. Crane told her about the Ashby diamonds. Forty years ago the old lady's brother had brought home a necklace of seven stones from India. The necklace had vanished on the night of his funeral, and nobody had seen it since. Dr. Crane said that half the village believed the diamonds were still somewhere in the house.

When the doctor had gone, Eleanor opened the box of letters at last. The first letter was addressed to the old lady and was signed only with a single initial, the letter A. It spoke of a debt, and of a promise, and of a ship that would come for what was owed.

Eleanor Vane did not tell Mr. Thorne what she had read. She put the letters back in their box, tied the black ribbon exactly as before, and went down to supper with her heart beating fast. Mr. Thorne served the soup in silence and watched her the whole time.

That night she lay awake and listened. The footsteps came again, slow and careful, going down toward the cellar.



CHAPTER III

THE DIAMONDS

On the last night of October a ship anchored below the cliff, and a man came up the path with a lantern. He was Captain Ashby, the old lady's nephew, and he had sailed from Bristol to collect a debt that was forty years old.

Captain Ashby was a broad, weathered man with a scar across his chin. He said that the necklace had been promised to his father, and that he had come to take it home. Eleanor told Captain Ashby about the footsteps and about the letters in the black ribbon.

Together they went down the narrow stair to the cellar. Behind a row of empty wine racks they found a loose stone, and behind the stone a leather bag. Inside the bag were seven white diamonds.

At that moment Mr. Thorne appeared on the stair with his lantern. He confessed that he had taken the diamonds on the night of the funeral and had hidden them in the wall, meaning to sell them one by one. Mr. Thorne was the thief, and he had been visiting his hiding place every night for forty years without ever daring to sell a single stone.

Dr. Crane was sent for in the morning. Captain Ashby took the diamonds to the old lady, who wept and said that her brother's promise was kept at last. Eleanor Vane finished the catalogue of the library before the first winter storm.
